A postal card was intercepted at the New York postoffice, directed "President Arthur, Washington, D. C." Upon the lower left hand corner was written, with a lead pencil, the word "Private." On the reverse was written:

"President Arthur:—If you do not recall the Minister from England and ask for the unconditional surrender of all Americans in English dungeons you shall be shot and killed."

Across these penned lines was written, with a black lead pencil:

"This is no idle boast. We mean business. You are no American."

It caused considerable excitement, but it is probably much more harmless than it was intended to appear and is only a stupid joke.

The stock reporter of the New York Times is a lady, Miss Mary Morgan, who has accumulated a handsome competency by her connection with the Times and Herald, to both of which she furnish reports of the live stock markets. She came to this country about fifteen years ago, and is an expert in all matters relating to cows, sheep, hogs, horses, and can tell the weight of a horned creature at a glance. Her knowledge of horses proved useful to her as a member of Victor Emanuel's staff, as she was intrusted with the duty of buying the horses for his army. A RAPIST ROPED.

CATLETTSBURG, Ky., June 4. — A body of masked men chartered a train of cars at Ashland Friday night, where the two girls in Gibbons' residence were murdered after they had been outraged, came here at 2:30 a.m. Saturday, went to the jail where George Ellis, one of the men on trial for the murder, was imprisoned, broke in and took him out to the scene of the murder and hanged him to a tree. Ellis, who had turned state's evidence, had been convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for life.

The body of George Ellis was left hanging. The coroner's jury held an inquest, but the crowd refused to allow it to be cut down. Mrs. Ellis went to Virginia before the lynching, and is yet ignorant of it.

DAILY POST-INTELLIGENCER.
PREVALENCE OF LYNCH LAW.
Lynch law hangings are almost daily reported, and from every part of the country. This indicates a deplorable condition of affairs, but it is one easily understood. There are entirely too many quirks and quibbles in the law. Judges are too often politicians, juries corrupt, witnesses bribed, and justice perverted. If a culprit has neither money nor friends he may stand a chance to get what he deserves, after a prolonged and tedious delay. If he has money or friends, or both, he will go clear by means of some dark work, or will be inadequately punished. The American people have shown great toleration in the past, but their patience has lately been taxed beyond the verge of endurance. A case in point is reported from Kentucky. Three fellows went after midnight to a house occupied by three young girls, outraged them, broke their heads with bars of iron, and then set fire to the house containing their bodies. It was one of the worst, most devilish acts ever perpetrated. There was but little doubt of the guilt of the men arrested, and an effort was made at the time by the maddened neighbors and relatives to capture and hang them. They have since all had trials and been convicted, but instead of being murder in the first degree the extent of their horrible act was declared to be manslaughter, the punishment for which would probably be a few years' imprisonment, followed by pardon. Upon this jury finding, the other day in the case of the last man tried, the people could no longer stand it, and they seized the murderer and promptly hung him. The people of Missouri, according to published reports, are about to have a legal outrage perpetrated upon them. It is said a compact has been made between the Governor of the State and Frank James, the notorious trainwrecker, bank robber, highwayman and murderer, by the terms of which the latter is to be given a full pardon for all his numerous past misdoeds simply on his promise to live a correct life hereafter. The failures and shortcomings of the law are evident on every hand, and it is not surprising that people are no longer willing to rely upon it for the punishment of the worst class of offenders. Only a month or two ago, in the large, sedate city of St. Paul the jail was broken open and a miscreant taken out and hung. Bloomington, Illinois, furnishes another illustration. As said before these things are deplorable, but there seems to be no help for them. This taking the law into one's own hands is no pleasant matter, and the people are invariably greatly wronged before they are led up to the pitch necessary to so violent an act. The law must do what it is made for, namely: protect the people and encourage the right, or the law will of necessity be set aside by those higher than it—its makers, the people.

Emma Thomas, Fannie Gibbons and Robbie Gibbons were the victims of the foul deed. A few days thereafter George Ellis voluntarily went went before a committee, consisting of A. Campbell, cashier of the Ashland National Bank, Colonel John Russell and John Calder, who had been selected by the citizens of Ashland to aid the detective in ferreting out the case, and voluntarily confessed to them that he and Ellis Craft and Wm. Neal
george-ellis-catlettsburg-1882-06-03.A23:
terrible crime. He claimed that he (Ellis) was an unwilling participant, having been forced by Craft and Neal to accompany them to the Gibbons cottage.

The three were arrested, and at a special term of our Circuit Court, held last January, they were indicted. At the same term Craft and Neal were put on trial, convicted and sentenced to be hanged. An appeal was taken to the Court of Appeals, where their cases are still pending. Ellis, Neal and Craft were sent to the Lexington jail, where they have remained, and where the two latter are still confined, Ellis having been brought here at the beginning of the present term of our Court for trial. On last Monday the trial of Ellis was begun, which terminated on Friday morning by the jury bringing in a verdict of guilty, and fixing his punishment at confinement in the Penitentiary for life. The people who were in attendance during the trial manifested a calm but earnest interest in the proceedings; and when the verdict was rendered it was thought that it would satisfy the most bloodthirsty. But the sequel shows there are those among us who believe in the Mosaic law of a life for a life.

This morning between one and two o'clock, a body of about sixty men, in disguise, appeared at the engine-house of the Chattarol Railroad Company in Ashland and took charge of the premises. They fired up an engine, brought it out on the track, hitched on two flat-cars and moved out of this place. They supplied their own engineer and brakemen. Their train arrived here about three o'clock. Halting upon the track opposite the jail, they moved upon the jail and demanded admittance, which was refused. They tried to force open the front door, but it did not yield readily to the pressure. They proceeded to a window in the jailor's residence (which is connected with the jail,) broke it in, and through it became masters of the situation. The jailor refused to give up the keys to the cell doors, but they were taken by force, and George Ellis was led out with the fatal halter around his neck. He was put on board the train, carried back to Ashland, and taken immediately in the rear of the premises where he had aided in the commission of the foulest crime known to civilization. He was hung to a sycamore tree, and permitted to hang until the County Coroner reached the scene, about nine o'clock this morning, and had the corpse cut down.

The news of the hanging spread rapidly through this place, Ashland and the surrounding neighborhood, and before the Coroner arrived perhaps more than a thousand people had visited the spot. Your correspondent arrived there about half-past seven o'clock. The crowd was then large, and continued to grow larger. The men composing the mob were so completely disguised that no one who saw them could recognize any one connected with it.

At the Coroner's inquest the jury decided that Ellis came to his death from the hands of unknown parties. The lynching seems satisfactory to the citizens of both Ashland and Catlettsburg

Our readers remember the Ashland horror, in Kentucky, about a year ago, when three men, after ravishing the Gibbons children, murdered them and tried to burn up their bodies by setting the house on fire. Three men—George Ellis, William Craft and Elias Neal—were proved to have been the guilty parties. Ashland, Ky., June 3.—At 2 o'clock this morning a mob of about thirty masked men entered the engine house of the Chataroi railroad at Ashland. Taking possession of one engine and four coaches, they made the watchman take a signal lantern and walk in front of the engine, and proceeded to Catlettsburg, five miles above here. Arriving there about 3 A.M., they marched to the jail, and, after being refused admittance, broke in the window and took the keys from Jailor Gullky. George Ellis, who was yesterday sentenced to the penitentiary for life for the murder of Robbie Gibbons, was taken out and carried to the train, which immediately returned to Ashland. There the crowd again disembarked and silently conveyed Ellis to the upper end of the town, where a large sycamore tree stood, close to where the Gibbons house (the scene of the murder) had been, and hanged him to a limb. The crowd then as silently dispersed, leaving the body of Ellis hanging to the tree, where it was found this morning, damp with the rain that had recently fallen, suspended about 2½ feet from the ground. He looked natural, with his eyes and mouth closed. It is evident that he was choked to death, as his neck is not broken. The limb was about ten feet from the ground, and the rope was about three-quarters of an inch thick, with a regular hangman's knot.

john-hanson-louisville-1882-06.A1:
RUGBY AS IT IS. No. II.
We will resume our walk around the town to "tell the towers thereof" by going along Lincoln street, which runs out of Central Avenue, from the Commissary. This street, until very lately, has been scarcely defined, and has existed more upon the map than anywhere else. The axe has been at work, though, and hewn a broad road, on which several excellent villa residences are built. We must notice first, however, the Brown House, a comfortable family hotel, and boarding house, of which Mr. James Milmow is the proprietor. This hotel gained its name, and much of its fame, from its first proprietor, Mr. Otis Brown, who, at the start of the colony, catered for the wants of the early adventurers. The hotel has a good, square, comfortable appearance, and pretty green outlook.

Across the road, diagonally, is Mr. Taylor's house, standing in a garden crowded with flowers, plants and vegetables, and showing how care, with a little manure, is richly rewarded with a healthy and bountiful yield, and proving, to demonstration, that the soil has been grossly libelled by those who have declared it unfit for cultivation. We have not been of late one who "into nobody's tater patch pokes," because, like a veritable Colorado beetle, we have been looking right and left among our neighbor's potato beds, and have not seen for general appearance—we have seen much larger beds—a richer, finer looking lot than is growing in Mr. Taylor's garden. This gentleman has also, across the road, lower down, a well fenced acre enclosure planted with potatoes and corn.

On Lincoln street, opposite Mr. Taylor's is Mr. Tucker's pretty suburban residence, standing in a very large garden, which is kept in very neat style. The situation is good, the house convenient, and everything about it suggestive of comfort, inside and out. In the rear of the house is a neat little home farm, with a paddock adjoining. Mr. Tucker is evidently an experimentalist. He is trying vines, raspberries, blackberries, tomatoes, fruit trees, strawberries, and a number of other products; and we anticipate a raid on his estate when the fruit is ripe, and the cream is about—and the proprietor ditto, of course. A large piece of grass in front of the house is growing and looking well.

A little lower down, on the brow of the hill, overlooking a world of trees, in a large, well filled, and attended garden, is Mr. Otis Brown's comfortable residence. This gentleman has plainly shown here his faith by his works, and we don't know that we can say much else. His work has been well done too. A few months ago the place was a wild, rough spot, with nothing to commend it but as the site for a house, and now the land has been most thoroughly cleaned, and the gently undulating part in front of the house laid down in grass, dotted with flower beds, a rockery, and the trappings of civilized nature.

"If we could do with this world of ours.

What thou dost with thy garden bowers,

Reject the weeds, and keep the flowers.

What a heaven on earth we'd make it!"

The rest of the garden is devoted to vegetable and fruit production. Mr. Brown has great faith in the capabilities of Rugby soil, and is a colonist of much energy. His sons, Mr. A. H. and Ross Brown, have struggled manfully with colonial work, and have gotten the upper hand. They are now subduing a piece of land in Fentress County, and preparing it for silk-worm culture.

We shall now take a leap of about a mile, to the other side of the town, to what is known as the "Savage Club," Mr. Hughes' farm—but is really a most civilized homestead, with a big piece of ground, every inch of which is under the rigid discipline of an energetic, hard-working, practical gardener—Mr. Charles Dyer. Last June he entered on the land, which presented a most rough and despairing condition, necessitating the grubbing out of one thousand trees. The amount of roots and rubbish cleared off was simply enormous. Now the ground is most thoroughly cleaned and producing a very large variety of vegetables, among which we noticed, tomatoes, potatoes, spinach, pears, cabbages, strawberries, beans, celery, turnips, beets, marrows, squashes, etc. This land was cultivated some years ago, but never properly farmed, and we question if it had ever any manure put into it. Mr. Dyer's success has been gained by great perseverance, untiring attention, and by "knowledge," which Lord Bacon truly declared to be "power." But little manure has been available, and it is simply astonishing to see such splended hills of potatoes, not tops only, but tubers already as big as your fist. Mr. Dyer's cucumbers have done, and are doing, well. A few samples, fifteen inches long, and about four in circumference, were sent to Cincinnati this week. The "Savage Club" is a roomy, comfortable house, and has been the home of many Rugbeians, seeking board and lodging. There is a large level clearing in the forest in front of the house, and a very pretty break in the great monotomy of trees it is, too, which is used frequently for foot-ball, and base-ball games, and may be said to be the field of the Rugby Isthmian Games.

Under an old law passed in 1795, a colored man, named John Hanson, was sentenced at Louisville, Kentucky, last Wednesday, to be sold into slavery for one year, as his punishment on a charge of vagrancy. Slavery Days Recalled.
A special despatch from Louisville, Ky., says: Memories of the ante-bellum days were recalled in a vivid manner to-day, in this city, by the sale into slavery for one year of John Hanson. John is, as the advertisement posted on the Court-house door states, "an able-bodied man of color, about 40 years of age, sound in every respect, with the exception of a rheumatic trouble of the lower limbs." Hanson was brought before a Justice's a few days ago and convicted of vagrancy. The Justice sent the case to the Circuit Court, where, under the provisions of a law passed in 1795, he was sentenced to be sold at public auction to the highest bidder for one year. The authority for this sentence is found in section 4 of the Vagrancy law of Kentucky, which reads as follows: "Persons indicted for vagrancy shall be tried by a jury, and if found guilty shall be sold into servitude for a period not exceeding one year." As Hanson's case was the first of the kind in this city since before the war, the announcement of his sale brought a large crowd together, in spite of a threatening storm, to witness the novel sight. A large number of negroes were present, and their comments on the sale were very amusing. One old darkey with frosty hair remarked: "Look out, white folks, look out; you start dis heah business again and there'll be another 'bellion, suah.' Another said: "Why dat niggah's no count; I wouldn't give five cents for him; I'd consider a nickel frowed away on him." At 12 o'clock the Sheriff made his appearance with the vagrant in tow. The latter was mounted on a chair. and sheepishly surveyed the crowd about him. Several men approached him, felt of his legs and arms, and asked him how much work he could do, and finally the bidding commenced. Fifty cents was the first offer, and for a while the bidding was lively, going up a nickel at a time until $1 15 was reached. Then there was a pause, and it looked as if the poor fellow would be knocked down at this figure, when a city scavenger offered two dollars, and no one bidding against him, secured his man. The negro said nothing to the hoots of the crowd, but meekly followed his master off. By the laws of the State the purchaser has the same power over his purchase as a master over a slave had before the war, and can wip him or use him in any manner he sees fit. The judge who sentenced Hanson says he is going to serve every vagrant who comes before him in the future in the same way. The negroes in the crowd were much excited, and thought it was too unpleasantly like old slave-time practices for comfort. As an illustration of the stagnation prevalent in Kentucky, this incident is particularly striking. That a law passed in the last century, and which is direct conflict with the laws and Constitution of the United States, should be enforced in a large city like Louisville and in this age, is not only remarkable, but strongly indicative of the non-progressive spirit which characterizes the Bourbon lawmakers of this typical Bourbon State.

TWICE IN A NIGHT.
The Number of Times Nigel Ned was Strung up.
Wednesday night a saloon keeper at Sherman discovered that four boxes of cigars had been stolen from his place. Suspicion settled on a colored man who is simply known by the name of Ned. This gentleman was caught and the missing cigars found in his possession. The party who caught the negro, in order to frighten him thoroughly, put a rope around his neck and strung him up for a moment or two. They then let him down and after offering him some sage advice about his conduct in the future, told him to depart. He did so, apparently in the direction of Laramie. This was about eleven o'clock.

Some time later, a barn located on the outskirts of Sherman was discovered on fire. Despite every effort made to stay the flamesit was burned to the ground together with a valuable horse which it contained. The fire was generally considered to be of incendiary origin and upon inquiry it was learned that "nigger" Ned had been seen in the vicinity and about the time the fire broke out had started in the direction of Cheyenne. Several parties immediately started on a hand car in this direction, but had only gone a few miles when they found their man secreted in some sheds. A rope was procured and the formalities of a lynching gone through with it, but although half choked the negro refused to confess that he had set the barn on fire. Finding it impossible to extract a confession, the men led him back to Sherman and turned him over to the authorities. It is probable he will be tried for arson.

True Inwardness of the Thing.
SHERMAN, Wyo., May 5.
In your issue of the 5th we find an article headed "Twice in a Night," etc. I beg leave to correct your reporter, who, I am sorry to say, was misinformed regarding our racket at Sherman Wednesday night. Nigger Ned has been employed by Mr. Pillman, proprietor of the Summit and Sherman house, as a chore boy, but of late he has been in the habit of stealing things whenever he got a good chance. On Wednesday a suit of clothes was found missing and five boxes of cigars. Ed was called to account. He claimed to be innocent but a rope was brought and Ed put it on his own neck. He said he wanted to have the thing done right. One end was placed over a telegraph pole and about ten men on Ed's end of the line and six on the other. Ed promised to tell where the things were if let go. So he led the way to part of the things. Then he promised to leave the place if liberated, but instead he only went a short distance below Sherman toward Laramie City and in an hour the barn belonging to the hotel with a valuable horse was burned and the hotel buildings only escaped by a large force of men carrying water from the tank close by and keeping everything wet down. Ed was discovered four miles east of Sherman in camp with a camper. He was taken back to Sherman and well treated and no hanging as stated. On his person was found one box of cigars which he admits was hid close to the barn. When found he had thrown away his shoes. He admitted that he was sorry for what he had done the night before. He had a hearing before Justice Roberts and was committed to jail in default of $500 bonds the October term of court.

Yours Respt.,
A. L. SUTHERLAND.

Two Citizens shot Down Yesterday without Cause or Provocation—One Is Mortally Wounded.

About 4:30 p. m. yesterday the lower business portion of the city was thrown into a state of extraordinary excitement by a tragic occurrence happening upon the public street. The excitement arose from the statement that James Lansing, a prominent and respected citizen, had been shot down upon the street and killed. The streets in the vicinity of Third, Fourth, K and L were immediately thronged with excited citizens, and it was with great difficulty that the officers of the law secured the would-be murderer, forced him into a hack and conveyed him to the city prison.

THE FACTS.

Simon Raten is a native of West Siberia, is an employee at the railroad shops, has been in this State six months. He has been drinking considerably of late. On Sunday he became involved in an altercation with a man by the name of Andrew Erickson. He followed Erickson around the greater part of the day trying to provoke a fight. Finally Erickson was forced to fight and gave Raten a very sound drubbing. Yesterday morning, fired with liquor and smarting under the humiliation of the sound flogging he had evidently justly received from Erickson, he procured a pistol and went out hunting for the latter, determined on revenge. At half-past four, Raten, while walking down street, met the object of his search coming up along the south side of K street, between Third and Fourth streets. Raten immediately drew a pistol and fired. Erickson, seeing the assassin approach, dodged as the pistol was fired and escaped the intended bullet. A young man named John J. Livingston, who was walking behind Erickson, received the shot in his right hand. The shot attracted immediate attention. The assassin turned at once back toward Fourth street from just in front of the office door of the International Hotel, and began to run. As he came to the corner of the street Richard Leslie attempted to intercept him, but he pointed the pistol at him and turned down Fourth street toward L. By this time a crowd was in pursuit of him. As he came to the alley between K and L he turned into it and ran toward Third street.

JAMES LANSING,
Who was in the back yard of his premises (the International Hotel), which open upon the alley, hearing the noise made by the people pursuing the assassin, and the cries of the officers, opened his gate and stepped into the alley just as Raten passed the gate. Lansing ran after the man a few feet, when the latter turned with his pistol in his hand. Lansing stopped short and threw up his hands, and some say he cried out, "Don't shoot." Raten was then about four feet from Lansing. He paid no heed to Lansing's protest, and fired. Lansing staggered back and re-entered his yard, and had strength sufficient to walk to the hotel, when he was assisted to his room. Raten stood a few seconds with his pistol pointed toward his pursuers, and then turned and ran on to Third street. He turned down Third toward L, and near L ceased running, and walked. Charles Heinrich, a grocer, met him there and asked him what was the matter. Raten replied, "I don't know v what they want of me." He then turned up L street and began to run. A few seconds later his pursuers were on him, and midway of the block he was overtaken, thrown, and made a prisoner.

A BOY'S STATEMENT.
Jacob Goldstein, aged 15, a newsboy, says he was in the alley when Raten entered it. He saw Mr. Lansing open his gate, and saw him put up his hands, as if to stop the man. Lansing, seeing the man with a pistol, cried out, "Don't shoot," but the man thrust the pistol close to Lansing's body and fired. Lansing reeled and staggered and "acted wildly," as the boy puts it, and cried out "I am shot." Raten then threw his pistol over a fence and ran toward Third street. The boy followed with the crowd in pursuit of Raten, who was overtaken on L street, near the middle of the roadway, and about halfway between Third and Fourth. The boy says Thomas Stevens and William Dolan were the first to seize the man, who resisted and had to be thrown to the ground. P. Brannigan, officer Campbell, and other officers were almost simultaneously on the spot, and to them the prisoner was turned over.

James Lansing, who was shot by Simon Raten Monday afternoon, died yesterday at 5 p. m. He lived about twenty-four hours after receiving the deadly wound. Mr. Lansing having been a member of the Exempt Firemen's Association, the bells of the Fire Department were tolled as soon as his death was known. SACRAMENTO, April 11. — James Lansing, shot by Raten on Monday, died last night. A crowd surrounded his hotel and subsequently went to the jail where Raten was confined. Fearing an attack and lynching, the Chief of Police called for military assistance, and four companies of the National Guard occupied the jail. simon-raten-sacramento-1882-04-11.A13:
THE RATEN TRIAL.
The trial of Raten, who murdered James Lansing, has been concluded in an eminently proper way, and with commendable speed. He was found guilty of murder in the first degree, just one month and two days after he committed the crime. The Court and the jury have therefore done their full duty, and it is to be hoped that sentence and execution will not be delayed. Sacramento has found two murderers guilty within two weeks, and a Sacramento Court in the first of these cases has by recurring to a commonsense interpretation of the Code taken a position the general adoption of which would unquestionably relieve our criminal administration of a great abuse. These two cases have gone far to indicate that it is no longer safe for the defense in murder cases to rely upon the plea of insanity, when a jury of any intelligence is impaneled. That plea has almost frustrated the purpose of the law for the protection of human life in many parts of the country, and it has loaded the Court records with scandals, of which we regret to be compelled to say that California has had somewhat more than her share. We hope, however, that the example set by a Sacramento Court and Sacramento juries will not be lost upon the rest of the State, but that these prompt judgments may stimulate other communities to convict and to execute justice upon their criminals, and to put an end to the sluggishness which in so many instances, and notably in San Francisco, allows murderers to crowd the County Jails, and to escape trial sometimes for years together.

IDENTITY OF THE WAVERLY MURDERER.

LINCOLN, Neb., February 23.—The discovery has been made that Ralvin, who is in the county jail for the murder of James Cook at Waverly Sunday night, is none other than the notorious Quin Bohanan, a former inmate of the penitentiary and a desperado whose name was once a terror along the Missouri river. While an inmate of the penitentiary Quin Bohanan and a man by the name of McWaters headed a revolt which was not quelled until the United States troops were called out and the prison surrounded. The mutiny lasted three days. Bohanan and McWaters took an active part in the revolt, showing unusual courage and nerve. McWaters was afterwards shot dead by a guard. Bohanan served out his time, and was discharged, since which time he has not been seen hereabouts until he appeared as the chief actor in the fiendish murder of Sunday night. Ralvin was arraigned for murder.

TORONTO, February 23.—In the J. R. Miller extradition case, judgment was reserved until to-morrow. The result of Mr. Murphy's visit to Ottawa was satisfactory, and it is not likely the prisoner will leave Canada, except under the guarantee that he will be tried only for the offense for which he may be extradited. Mr. Murphy received a telegram from Mr. Hill, who instituted the proceedings, saying that Mr. Connors had been deceived, and that the only true affidavit is that presented by Detective Kribbs, which Judge McKenzie would not recognize. From this, it is apparent that Miller will have to return to Canada in the event of his extradition. Miller himself says he had nothing to do with the robbery.
